framework.title: Core Values Exploration Reference Framework
framework.purposeSummary: The editorial brief the individual value write-ups are authored against. Not user-facing content.
notes: Body text is verbatim from the source document. Inline emphasis is preserved as markdown.
explorationChecklist is the list of lenses at the head of the document.
standardStructure is the twenty-two point authoring spec.
lenses, discernmentQuestions and alignmentTest are structured extracts of material also present in the blocks.

lenses.question: What did the word originally mean?
From what linguistic, philosophical, religious, or cultural tradition did the concept emerge?
What does the value represent as a motivational or behavioral orientation?
How has the underlying principle been understood within contemplative, ethical, mystical, or wisdom traditions?
What might the value mean when understood through consciousness, relationship, interconnectedness, being, or one's orientation toward reality?
What does this value actually look like when someone lives it?
How can someone distinguish genuine alignment from identification with the *idea* of the value?

standardStructure.title: VALUE
blocks: The word being explored.

standardStructure.title: CORE DEFINITION
blocks: A concise contemporary definition of the value.
This section establishes what the word generally means before examining the deeper layers surrounding it.

standardStructure.title: ETYMOLOGY
blocks: Explore:
**Root language:** Latin, Greek, Old English, Sanskrit, French, Germanic, or another linguistic origin.
**Original word:** The earliest relevant linguistic form.
**Literal meaning:** What the root originally communicated.
**Evolution:** How the word's meaning changed as it moved through languages, historical periods, religions, philosophies, or cultures.
Where useful, distinguish between the historical meaning and the way modern psychology or spirituality uses the term.

standardStructure.title: HISTORICAL AND CONCEPTUAL ORIGIN
blocks: Explore the broader history of the *concept*, rather than merely the English word.
Questions include:
Where does this idea appear historically?
Did Greek philosophy discuss an equivalent virtue?
Does Hindu philosophy contain a related principle?
Does Buddhism approach the concept differently?
Does Taoism provide another interpretation?
Does Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Indigenous philosophy, Stoicism, or another tradition contain a related principle?
Did psychology later reinterpret the concept?
The English word and the human principle may have very different histories.

For example, the English word **equanimity** has a Latin linguistic history, while the cultivation of profound equanimity appears independently within Buddhist contemplative traditions through *upekkhā*.
These parallels should be explored without claiming that historically unrelated traditions necessarily borrowed from one another.

standardStructure.title: ORIGINAL OR INTENDED USE
blocks: Examine how the word was originally used.
Was it primarily:
a moral virtue,
a religious principle,
a description of character,
a social expectation,
a philosophical concept,
a psychological quality,
a political concept,
an economic concept,
or something else?
Then compare this with contemporary usage.
This is particularly important for words whose meanings have shifted substantially.

standardStructure.title: PSYCHOLOGICAL MEANING
blocks: Examine the value as an organizing principle of human behavior.
Consider:
What psychological need might this value express?
What behaviors does it tend to motivate?
What emotional experiences accompany alignment with it?
How might the value influence decision making?
How might it affect relationships?
How might it influence identity?
How might childhood conditioning influence someone's relationship with this value?
Could the person have inherited this value from family, religion, culture, socioeconomic environment, trauma, or social expectations?
Is the value freely chosen, or merely internalized?
This distinction matters because an inherited rule can masquerade as a personal value.

standardStructure.title: SPIRITUAL MEANING
blocks: Explore how the value can function as a principle of spiritual development.
Depending upon the particular value, relevant traditions may include:
Buddhism,
Hinduism,
Vedānta,
Yoga philosophy,
Taoism,
Jainism,
Christian mysticism,
Jewish mysticism,
Sufism,
Stoicism,
Neoplatonism,
Indigenous traditions,
and contemporary contemplative spirituality.
The objective is not to force every value into every spiritual tradition.
Instead, identify genuine conceptual parallels where they exist.
Questions may include:
How does this value affect one's relationship with self?
How does it affect one's relationship with other beings?
How does it affect one's relationship with suffering?
How does it affect one's relationship with ego?
How does it affect one's relationship with impermanence?
How does it affect one's relationship with the sacred?
Does the value encourage greater separation or greater recognition of interconnectedness?

standardStructure.title: METAPHYSICAL INTERPRETATION
blocks: This section explores the value philosophically rather than presenting metaphysical propositions as experimentally established facts.
Questions may include:
What does this value imply about the nature of self?
What does it imply about agency?
What does it imply about consciousness?
What does it imply about interconnectedness?
What does it imply about our relationship with reality?
What happens when consciousness organizes itself around this principle?
Does the value move someone toward contraction or expansion?
Toward separation or relationship?
Toward control or participation?
Toward identification or observation?
Toward resistance or acceptance?
Toward fragmentation or coherence?
The metaphysical interpretation should remain distinct from scientific claims.
For example:
Rather than:
“Integrity raises your vibrational frequency.”
A more epistemically careful exploration would be:
“Within energetic and metaphysical frameworks, integrity can be understood as a state of greater coherence because thought, speech, intention, and behavior are moving in the same direction.”
The second statement preserves the metaphysical framework without presenting an unmeasured physical frequency as established science.

standardStructure.title: THE EMBODIED EXPRESSION
blocks: This section answers:
**What does this value look like when it becomes behavior?**
Identify concrete manifestations.
For example, someone who values **integrity** might:
keep commitments,
correct themselves when they are wrong,
tell difficult truths compassionately,
decline opportunities that violate their principles,
behave similarly when nobody is watching,
and accept consequences rather than manipulate reality to protect their image.
This transforms an abstract noun into observable behavior.

standardStructure.title: INTERNAL EXPERIENCE OF ALIGNMENT
blocks: Explore what alignment may feel like internally.
Possible experiences include:
congruence,
clarity,
steadiness,
peace,
vitality,
openness,
self respect,
groundedness,
reduced internal negotiation,
or willingness to tolerate discomfort in service of what matters.
Importantly, alignment should **not** automatically be equated with comfort.
Living according to a value may create discomfort.
Courage may involve fear.
Honesty may involve vulnerability.
Boundaries may produce guilt.
Justice may require confrontation.
Authenticity may create rejection.
Compassion may require grief.
Therefore:
**Discomfort does not necessarily indicate misalignment. Sometimes discomfort is the price of alignment.**

standardStructure.title: BEHAVIORAL EVIDENCE OF ALIGNMENT
blocks: This should become one of the strongest sections of every value exploration.
Ask:
Where can this value be observed in behavior?
What decisions demonstrate it?
What sacrifices demonstrate it?
What boundaries protect it?
Where does the person choose it when another option would be easier?
What happens when living this value costs them approval, comfort, money, status, convenience, or belonging?
A useful principle is:
**Values become visible under pressure.**
It is easy to value kindness when everyone is kind to us.
The deeper question is what happens to kindness when we encounter someone difficult.
It is easy to value integrity when honesty costs nothing.
The revealing moment comes when truth carries consequences.

standardStructure.title: SIGNS OF MISALIGNMENT
blocks: Identify behavioral contradictions.
These might include:
repeatedly acting contrary to the stated value,
resentment,
chronic self betrayal,
internal fragmentation,
rationalization,
performative identification,
outsourcing responsibility,
compulsive approval seeking,
avoidance,
or repeatedly choosing short term relief over the stated principle.
The important distinction is between occasional human inconsistency and persistent contradiction.
Alignment does not require perfection.
It requires a recognizable orientation.

standardStructure.title: THE SHADOW EXPRESSION
blocks: Every value deserves this section.
A psychologically healthy value can become distorted when driven by fear, ego protection, trauma, social conditioning, or rigid identification.
Examples:
**Compassion → self abandonment**
**Strength → emotional suppression**
**Independence → inability to receive support**
**Peace → conflict avoidance**
**Service → martyrdom**
**Loyalty → tolerating abuse**
**Discipline → rigidity**
**Freedom → avoidance of commitment**
**Generosity → compulsive giving**
**Detachment → emotional disengagement**
**Spirituality → spiritual bypassing**
**Non judgment → unwillingness to exercise discernment**
**Surrender → passivity**
**Acceptance → resignation**
**Humility → self diminishment**
**Confidence → superiority**
**Boundaries → emotional walls**
**Selflessness → disappearance of self**
This distinction prevents the exercise from becoming simplistic.
A value is not automatically healthy merely because the word sounds virtuous.

standardStructure.title: VALUE VERSUS DEFENSE MECHANISM
blocks: Ask:
**Am I moving toward something meaningful, or away from something frightening?**
Someone may call isolation **independence**.
Someone may call hypervigilance **discernment**.
Someone may call people pleasing **kindness**.
Someone may call emotional shutdown **detachment**.
Someone may call perfectionism **excellence**.
Someone may call control **responsibility**.
Someone may call avoidance **peace**.
Someone may call scarcity **prudence**.
Someone may call superiority **self respect**.
Someone may call dissociation **spiritual transcendence**.
The behavior alone cannot always reveal the value.
Its **function, motivation, flexibility, and consequences** must also be examined.

standardStructure.title: INHERITED VALUE VERSUS CHOSEN VALUE
blocks: Explore whether the value originated through:
family,
religion,
culture,
gender expectations,
economic conditions,
schooling,
community,
trauma,
social class,
professional identity,
media,
or conscious personal examination.
Then ask:
**If nobody rewarded me for embodying this value, would I still choose it?**
**If nobody knew I lived according to it, would it still matter to me?**
**If this value caused someone to disapprove of me, would I still recognize it as mine?**
These questions help distinguish intrinsic valuation from social compliance.

standardStructure.title: VALUE CONFLICTS
blocks: Values rarely operate independently.
They sometimes collide.
Freedom may conflict with commitment.
Honesty may conflict with kindness.
Security may conflict with adventure.
Individuality may conflict with belonging.
Peace may conflict with justice.
Loyalty may conflict with integrity.
Achievement may conflict with wellbeing.
Generosity may conflict with boundaries.
Tradition may conflict with innovation.
Self reliance may conflict with community.
The important question is therefore not merely:
**What do I value?**
It is also:
**Which value takes precedence when two of my values compete?**
Those moments reveal the actual hierarchy of someone's values.

standardStructure.title: RELATIONAL EXPRESSION
blocks: Explore how the value appears within relationships.
Ask:
How do I offer this value to others?
How do I allow others to offer it to me?
What boundaries arise from it?
What expectations arise from it?
Do I demand this value from others while exempting myself?
Do I extend it toward others while withholding it from myself?
What happens when someone I love does not share this value?

standardStructure.title: SELF RELATIONSHIP
blocks: Turn the value inward.
Someone may value:
compassion toward others but not themselves,
forgiveness toward others but not themselves,
freedom for themselves but not others,
honesty from others but not themselves,
respect from others while engaging in self contempt,
or generosity toward others while chronically depriving themselves.
Therefore ask:
**Does my relationship with myself reflect this value too?**

standardStructure.title: SOMATIC AND EMBODIED INQUIRY
blocks: Without claiming that bodily sensations provide infallible truth, the body can be used as another source of information.
Explore:
What happens in the body when the person honors this value?
What happens when they violate it?
Does the body become tense?
Open?
Contracted?
Restless?
Grounded?
Activated?
Quiet?
What sensations arise when imagining choosing this value despite social consequences?
The objective is not to declare:
“My body says this is true.”
Instead:
**“What information is my body contributing to this inquiry?”**

standardStructure.title: QUESTIONS FOR DISCERNMENT
blocks: Each value can conclude with several inquiries.
**Recognition**
What does this value mean to me personally?
**Origin**
Where did I learn that this mattered?
**Choice**
Would I consciously choose this value today?
**Evidence**
Where does my behavior demonstrate this value?
**Contradiction**
Where does my behavior contradict it?
**Cost**
What am I willing to sacrifice to live according to it?
**Shadow**
What unhealthy behavior could masquerade as this value?
**Relationship**
How does this value influence the way I treat other beings?
**Self**
Do I extend this value toward myself?
**Future Self**
How would embodying this value more completely change the way I live?

standardStructure.title: ALIGNMENT TEST
blocks: A useful final assessment for every value:
**I SAY I VALUE IT**
Is the value primarily conceptual?
**I FEEL DRAWN TOWARD IT**
Does it carry personal emotional significance?
**I CHOOSE ACCORDING TO IT**
Does it influence decisions?
**I BEHAVE ACCORDING TO IT**
Is there observable evidence?
**I PROTECT IT**
Do my boundaries preserve it?
**I ACCEPT ITS COST**
Am I willing to experience appropriate discomfort to remain aligned with it?
**I EXTEND IT CONSISTENTLY**
Does it appear across contexts rather than only when convenient?
**I CAN HOLD IT FLEXIBLY**
Can I embody it without turning it into rigidity, superiority, avoidance, or self punishment?
The final question becomes:
**Is this a word I admire, an identity I claim, or a principle I actually live?**

standardStructure.title: FUTURE SELF EXPRESSION
blocks: For values identified as aspirational rather than currently embodied:
What would this value look like if integrated?
What behaviors would change?
What boundaries would change?
What relationships might change?
What would the person stop tolerating?
What would they begin practicing?
What difficult conversation might become necessary?
What habit would become incompatible with the value?
What would become possible?
The purpose is not to imagine a perfect future identity.
It is to identify the **next observable expression of the value**.
A future value becomes embodied through present behavior.

parts.title: Purpose of the Reference Material
blocks: Each value should be explored as more than a definition.
The purpose is to investigate the word through several distinct lenses:
**Language:** What did the word originally mean?
**History:** From what linguistic, philosophical, religious, or cultural tradition did the concept emerge?
**Psychology:** What does the value represent as a motivational or behavioral orientation?
**Spirituality:** How has the underlying principle been understood within contemplative, ethical, mystical, or wisdom traditions?
**Metaphysics:** What might the value mean when understood through consciousness, relationship, interconnectedness, being, or one's orientation toward reality?
**Embodiment:** What does this value actually look like when someone lives it?
**Discernment:** How can someone distinguish genuine alignment from identification with the *idea* of the value?
This final distinction is essential.
A person may sincerely say, “I value compassion,” while repeatedly treating themselves with contempt.
Someone may value freedom while controlling everyone around them.
Someone may value peace while avoiding every necessary conflict.
Someone may value spirituality while using spiritual beliefs to avoid grief, anger, accountability, or material reality.
Therefore, stated values and enacted values are not necessarily the same.
The central inquiry becomes:
**If this is truly one of my values, where is the evidence of it in the way I live?**

parts.title: POLARITY AND TRANSCENDENCE
blocks: Every value exists within a larger field of human experience. Many values have an apparent opposite, shadow, tension, or contrasting state through which we come to understand the value more deeply.
We may recognize peace because we have experienced conflict.
We understand freedom partly through experiences of restriction.
We discover authenticity through noticing where we perform.
We recognize connection through experiences of separation.
We understand courage because fear exists.
We recognize abundance partly because we know the experience of scarcity.
From a nondual and transcendental perspective, however, these polarities do not need to be divided into categories of **good and bad**.
The unwanted pole is not necessarily evidence that something has gone wrong.
It is not punishment.
It is not spiritual failure.
It does not necessarily mean that we are misaligned, vibrating incorrectly, manifesting badly, or failing at consciousness.
Sometimes it is simply an experience arising within the totality of human consciousness.
The polarity can become a point of contrast through which awareness discovers itself, its preferences, its conditioning, and the direction in which it consciously desires to move.

parts.title: POLARITY AS CONTRAST
blocks: Contrast gives definition to experience.

Without darkness, our conceptual understanding of light would be incomplete. Without contraction, expansion becomes difficult to recognize. Without separation, we may never consciously contemplate unity.
The purpose of exploring polarity is therefore not to reject one side and cling to the other.
It is to become conscious of the relationship between them.
For each value, we can ask:
**What is the apparent polarity of this value?**
**What does experiencing that polarity reveal?**
**What becomes visible through the contrast?**
**What does the experience help me recognize that I desire to create, embody, or move toward?**
**Can I receive the information contained within the experience without condemning the experience itself?**

parts.title: POLARITY IS NOT PUNISHMENT
blocks: When an experience is painful, uncomfortable, unwanted, or disruptive, the human mind often moves immediately into interpretation:
**This should not be happening.**
**Something has gone wrong.**
**I have failed.**
**I attracted something bad.**
**I am out of alignment.**
**The universe is punishing me.**
**I need to get back into a higher state.**
A transcendental perspective invites another possibility:
**The experience is already here. Before deciding what it means, can we allow it to be what it is?**
Pain may be present.
Fear may be present.
Anger may be present.
Loss may be present.
Uncertainty may be present.
Contraction may be present.
None of these experiences requires us to construct an identity or cosmology around their existence.
The experience itself and our interpretation of the experience are not necessarily the same thing.
We can therefore distinguish:
**What happened.**
**What I experienced.**
**What I felt.**
**What I decided it meant.**
**What I now choose to create in relationship to it.**
This creates space between experience and interpretation.
And within that space, consciousness gains choice.

parts.title: DISCOMFORT AS INFORMATION
blocks: Discomfort is not inherently evidence of misalignment.
Sometimes discomfort reveals misalignment.
Sometimes discomfort accompanies profound alignment.
Setting a boundary can feel uncomfortable.
Leaving an unhealthy relationship can feel terrifying.
Telling the truth can produce anxiety.
Choosing authenticity can threaten belonging.
Grieving can feel unbearable while simultaneously representing deep love.
Changing an inherited belief can destabilize identity.
Standing for justice can create conflict.
Surrender can initially feel like losing control.
Detachment can feel frightening to a mind accustomed to securing itself through attachment.
Therefore, the question is not simply:
**Does this feel good or bad?**
A deeper inquiry is:
**What is this experience revealing?**

parts.title: THE NONDUAL INQUIRY
blocks: At the level of ordinary human experience, distinctions matter.
We experience pleasure and pain, expansion and contraction, connection and separation, safety and threat.
At the level of nondual inquiry, however, we can ask what contains all of these experiences.
What is aware of fear?
What is aware of peace?
What notices contraction?
What notices expansion?
What remains present while experiences change?
From this perspective, the work is not necessarily to destroy one polarity so that we can permanently inhabit another.
It is to become increasingly conscious of the awareness within which both poles arise.
We can still consciously choose peace.
We can choose compassion.
We can choose integrity.
We can choose freedom.
We can choose love.
But our choice no longer requires us to condemn everything that is not peace, compassion, integrity, freedom, or love.
We can move toward what we desire without declaring war against what revealed the desire.

parts.title: TRANSCENDING THE POLARITY
blocks: Transcendence does not necessarily mean escaping the human experience.
Nor does it require becoming indifferent to suffering, injustice, harm, or consequence.
Transcendence can instead mean developing the capacity to **hold the polarity without becoming completely identified with either side of it**.
We can experience fear without becoming Fear.
We can experience anger without becoming Anger.
We can experience scarcity without constructing scarcity as our identity.
We can experience separation while remembering interconnectedness.
We can encounter uncertainty without demanding that reality immediately resolve itself.
We can recognize an unwanted experience without needing to call the experience morally bad simply because we would not consciously choose more of it.
The experience becomes something consciousness can witness, learn through, respond to, and integrate.

parts.title: POLARITY AS A CREATIVE COMPASS
blocks: The unwanted experience can clarify desire.
**Restriction may reveal our longing for freedom.**
**Chaos may reveal our desire for groundedness.**
**Dishonesty may illuminate the importance of truth.**
**Disconnection may awaken our longing for intimacy.**
**Control may reveal our desire for surrender.**
**Judgment may reveal our desire for compassion.**
**Scarcity may clarify our relationship with abundance.**
**Noise may reveal our longing for stillness.**
**Fragmentation may awaken our remembrance of wholeness.**
In this way, polarity does not merely tell us what to escape.
It can show us where consciousness desires to move.
The inquiry becomes:
**Now that I have experienced this, what has it helped me know more clearly?**
And then:
**What do I consciously choose to create more of?**

parts.title: THE TRANSCENDENTAL DISTINCTION
blocks: There is an important difference between **preference** and **judgment**.
We can prefer one experience without condemning its opposite.
We can choose peace without declaring conflict cosmically wrong.
We can choose abundance without shaming ourselves for experiencing scarcity.
We can choose connection without making periods of solitude or separation evidence of spiritual failure.
We can choose courage while allowing fear to exist.
We can choose joy without requiring ourselves to remain joyful.
We can choose love without denying anger, grief, disappointment, or pain.
This allows values to become **directions of conscious creation rather than instruments of self judgment**.

parts.title: QUESTIONS FOR EACH VALUE
blocks: When exploring the polarity of a particular value, consider:
**What is the apparent opposite or polarity of this value?**
**Have I labeled one side good and the other bad?**
**What experiences taught me that distinction?**
**What does the unwanted polarity allow me to recognize about what I desire?**
**What does my discomfort reveal without requiring me to make the discomfort wrong?**
**Am I moving toward this value because I genuinely desire it, or because I am running away from its opposite?**
**Can I allow the unwanted pole to exist without allowing it to unconsciously govern my behavior?**
**What changes when I stop asking, “Why is this happening to me?” and begin asking, “What is this showing me?”**
**Can I consciously choose one direction without rejecting the totality of my human experience?**
**What would it mean to transcend identification with both poles while still consciously choosing how I want to live?**

parts.title: CORE PRINCIPLE
blocks: **Polarity gives us contrast. Contrast gives us information. Information creates the possibility of conscious choice.**
The objective is not to eradicate every experience we do not prefer.
It is to become conscious enough to recognize what the experience reveals, compassionate enough not to condemn ourselves for having it, and intentional enough to choose what we desire to embody next.
The polarity is not necessarily the enemy of the value.
Sometimes it is the very experience through which the value becomes visible.
And transcendence is not the rejection of either side.
It is the widening of consciousness until both can be seen from a place spacious enough to choose without condemnation.
